report:
Feature 15 is in: a server killed at any point now sends each account the note was shared with exactly one notification per archiving that was saved. The gate (`--base f3ddb77 --mode architecture --fix`) passes, and the work is committed on the current branch as `d4709b2`, not pushed. The API is unchanged.

**What was broken.** An archiving travels through three transactions: the archive itself, Notes passing it on, and Notifications creating the notifications. A crash at three points broke that chain:
- **A message could be lost.** A message waiting to be sent out (in the outbox) was marked sent as soon as the event bus took it, before anything had acted on it. A crash at that moment lost it.
- **A message could be doubled.** The record of which handler had already processed which message lived only in memory. After a restart a message was sent again, Notes would forward it under a new id, and recipients got two notifications.
- **Startup skipped the transactional path.** Messages re-sent at startup were handled without a transaction, so what Notes forwarded skipped the outbox.

**What changed.** These are changes to the shared building blocks, not a new context or relationship, so no storm was needed:
- **Durable record of handled messages.** A new `Inbox` (`src/Architecture/Application/Inbox.ts`) is stored in memory or in a SQLite table, alongside the data. Each event handler checks it inside its own transaction and skips a message it has already handled. Otherwise it writes the record in the same transaction as its own changes, so the two are saved together or not at all.
- **Messages marked sent only after delivery.** A waiting message is marked sent only once every handler has finished with it and none failed. A message still being handled isn't sent a second time in the meantime, and one whose handler failed waits for the next send.
- **Startup goes through a transaction.** The re-send at startup now runs each handler in a transaction of its own, like any other.
- **The drill.** It lives only in `src/Bootstrap/storage.ts`, and no context knows about it. With `FAULT_DRILL=after-archive`, the server sends itself `SIGKILL` right after the save that stores an archiving.
- **ADR.** The decision is recorded in `docs/adr/0006-notices-survive-a-crash.md`, and ADR 5's note that this record lived only in memory is amended.

**Tests.**
- `src/Bootstrap/Fastify/crash.e2e.spec.ts` starts the real server on a SQLite file with port 23300, archives a note shared with two people, and checks the drill killed the process. It then restarts it three times and checks each recipient has exactly one notification, and that the owner and an unrelated account have none.
- That test cuts the power before anything is passed on, so on its own it probably doesn't catch the doubling. Two unit specs cover the other crash points:
  - `SqliteInbox.spec.ts`: a message handled once is skipped even after reopening the database file, and a failed handler records nothing.
  - `Outbox.spec.ts`: a message stays waiting while its handler runs, isn't sent twice, and is kept when its handler fails.

**What was unclear, and what I decided:**
- **"First archiving it records."** I took it as the first save that adds an archiving to the outbox. The process dies there, so there is never a second one.
- **"An archiving that was not recorded gives no notification."** This already holds, because the archive and its event are saved together. I didn't add a drill for it.
- **Tokens across restarts.** The crash test sets `TOKEN_SECRET` and logs in again after each restart; otherwise tokens don't survive a restart (ADR 5).
- **Known limits**, written down in ADR 6:
  - The handled-messages table grows by one row per handled message and nothing prunes it.
  - A handler that keeps failing is retried after every save.
  - Handlers are told apart by class name.
  - Whether a message was delivered is worked out from status flags that all handlers share. If two handlers finish at nearly the same moment, the result could be misread. A false "failed" only causes a harmless re-send. A false "delivered" would drop the retry for a handler that failed, but it can't happen in the drill, where Notes' reaction doesn't fail.

Feature 16 is in: changes to one note sent at the same moment are all kept, whether the app runs as one process or as several processes on one SQLite file. The gate (`--base d4709b2 --mode architecture --fix`) passes, and the work is committed on the current branch as `087fda6`, not pushed. The API is unchanged.

**Where it stood before.** No change could be lost, because each save already checks the note's version, refuses a stale one, and retries up to three times. Three things still fell short:
- **Refusals in one process.** Without a database file, simultaneous transactions overlapped. Twenty shares read the same version, so most conflicted and some could run out of retries.
- **A second process failed outright.** It hit the other process's write lock and answered 500. I wrote the two-process test first, and it failed this way.
- **Tracker records could vanish.** A Tracker record (the operation a client polls) could be written into another request's open transaction and disappear if that request was refused.

**What changed.** These are building-block changes, recorded in ADR 7; there is no new context or relationship, so no storm:
- **Transactions take turns in memory too**, as they already did on SQLite. Each transaction reads what the previous one saved, so simultaneous changes are decided one after another instead of conflicting. The version check stays as the safety net.
- **Several processes on one file:**
  - The file now uses SQLite's write-ahead log, so reads never wait and see what any process saved straight away.
  - A process waiting for another's write lock retries after short pauses, so it keeps serving other requests meanwhile. After 30 seconds it gives up, and the change is refused with `ERROR`.
  - The version is read while the lock is held, so the check also holds across processes.
- **Tracker records are written twice:** once immediately, so the operation is there when the client first asks, and again in a transaction of their own. A rollback the first write happened to land in can't take the record away. My first version wrote only the second time, which broke the "record is there immediately" behaviour (five e2e tests failed), so I changed it.
- **Already in place from ADR 6:** the outbox and the record of handled messages live in the shared file. Whichever process sends a pending message out, each handler acts on it once.

**Tests:**
- `src/Bootstrap/Fastify/concurrency.e2e.spec.ts` runs two scenarios in one process, then again against two real server processes behind a round-robin proxy. The scenarios are twenty shares sent at once, which must all succeed and all be on the note, and an edit plus a share sent at once, which must both be kept. A third test checks that one process answers at once what the other recorded.
- It passed three runs in a row.
- `SqliteStorage.spec.ts` gains a case with two connections on one file: one waits for the other's lock without blocking, then sees its committed write.

**What was unclear, and what I decided:**
- **Tokens.** The product says a token from one process need not work with another. The two-process test still gives both servers the same `TOKEN_SECRET`, as a real deployment would, because a round-robin proxy would otherwise send a token to the wrong process. The app still signs tokens per process when no secret is set.
- **Ports.** Both servers and the proxy in the concurrency test take ports chosen by the OS, not 23300. Jest runs test files in parallel, and the crash test from feature 15 already uses 23300.
- **Refusals.** I didn't add a test that forces a refusal, because waiting for the lock now leaves almost nothing to conflict. The version check and the "refusal changes nothing" behaviour are covered by the existing repository and handler tests.
- **Costs**, recorded in ADR 7:
  - Writes are one at a time across all processes on the file.
  - A write outside a transaction (marking a message as sent, the immediate Tracker write) may freeze its process for up to 5 seconds while another process holds the lock.
  - Each process has its own event bus, so a message is handled by whichever process sends it out.

Feature 17 is in: with `NOTIFY_URL` set, every notification is also sent to the outside service and sent again until it is accepted, including after a crash. The gate (`--base 087fda6 --mode architecture --fix`) passes, and the work is committed on the current branch as `d7c882b`, not pushed. No route changes, and without `NOTIFY_URL` nothing is sent.

**How it works.** No new context or relationship was needed: the service is a channel the Notifications context sends through. The decision is recorded in ADR 8.
- **What is owed lives on the notification.** A notification created while `NOTIFY_URL` is set is marked as owed to the service, in the same transaction that creates it. When the service accepts it, the notification is marked accepted and records a `NotificationDeliveredOutside` event. Because this is stored rather than kept in memory, a crash loses nothing. Notifications stored before this change owe nothing.
- **What gets sent.** Only owed notifications that have come are sent: a reminder at its moment, never a cancelled one. The body is `{ id, recipientId, kind, noteId }`, with the same `id` that `GET /notifications` lists.
- **The connection to the service.** An HTTP adapter posts that body with a 2-second timeout. An error status, a network failure and a timeout all count as "not accepted".
- **Sending and retrying.** A delivery service in Notifications sends what is owed outside any transaction, so a slow service never holds the database. It records an acceptance in a transaction of its own. After a refusal it waits 250 ms, then 0.5, 1 and 2 seconds, then every 2.5 seconds. That puts the first retry within a second, and two sendings at most about 4.5 seconds apart, timeout included. One process never sends the same notification twice at once.
- **The timer.** The composition root runs a delivery pass every 100 ms when `NOTIFY_URL` is set, and stops it when the server stops.

**Tests:**
- Unit tests for the aggregate cover owed, accepted, a second acceptance changing nothing, and old stored notifications owing nothing.
- Unit tests for the delivery service cover: only owed notifications are sent, with the right body; nothing is sent again after acceptance; the retry timing over six refusals; reminders sent at their moment and never once cancelled; no simultaneous double send.
- `src/Bootstrap/Fastify/outside.e2e.spec.ts` runs real server processes against a fake service:
  - **Unreliable service:** it refuses, then doesn't answer within 2 seconds, then refuses, then accepts. All four sendings carry the same body with the listed id. The first retry comes within a second, the gaps stay at most 5 seconds, and nothing is sent after acceptance.
  - **Crash:** the service refuses, the server is killed with `SIGKILL`, and the notification is sent again after the restart. Once accepted, it isn't sent after another restart.

**What was unclear, and what I decided:**
- **Notifications from before `NOTIFY_URL` is set.** I decided they are never sent, even if the server is later started with it; otherwise turning the service on would flood it with history. A notification created while it was set waits for the next start that has it.
- **Reminders.** I took "receives" to mean a reminder is sent at its moment, as it appears in the list then, and never if cancelled.
- **Several processes on one file (feature 16).** Each process runs its own delivery, so two may send the same notification at the same moment under the same id. The product says that is harmless.
- **No storm file.** I wrote no storm file: nothing changes in the API, and the only new domain fact is the acceptance event.
- **Ports.** The servers and the fake service in the e2e test use ports chosen by the OS, not 23300, because the crash test from feature 15 already uses 23300 and test files run in parallel.
